prompt: What happens to a virtual thread's carrier when the virtual thread calls `Thread.sleep`?

choices.text: It is handed to the common fork-join pool used by parallel streams
choices.why: The scheduler has a pool of its own.

choices.text: It sleeps too, until the virtual thread wakes
choices.why: That is pinning, which `sleep` does not cause.

choices.text: The operating system destroys it and makes a new one later
choices.why: Carriers live as long as the scheduler.

choices.text: It runs another virtual thread
choices.why: Right: the sleeper's stack waits in the heap.

prompt: How many carriers does the virtual-thread scheduler use by default on this machine, and why?
hint: What do carriers need a processor for?

choices.text: One per virtual thread, created on demand
choices.why: Then virtual threads would be platform threads.

choices.text: Four, one per processor: only computing needs one
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Three, the common pool's size
choices.why: That is a different pool.

choices.text: Two hundred, to cover the waiting
choices.why: Waiting needs no carrier at all.

prompt: `Thread.currentThread().is___()` tells code whether it runs on a virtual thread.
A million virtual threads were running. How many more operating-system threads did the process have than before?
Why should virtual threads never be put in a fixed pool?

choices.text: A pool would pin them to carriers
choices.why: Pooling and pinning are unrelated.

choices.text: A pool reuses something expensive, and they are cheap
choices.why: Right; a pool would only bring back the queue.

choices.text: Pools only accept `Runnable`, not `Callable`
choices.why: Lesson 16's pools took both.

choices.text: The JVM refuses to reuse a virtual thread
choices.why: Nothing refuses; it is simply pointless.

prompt: Each of the million threads slept two seconds, yet the last finished 9.5 seconds after the first started. What does the lesson conclude?

choices.text: The executor ran them in batches of a thousand
choices.why: It gives each task its own thread at once.

choices.text: Virtual threads oversleep by design
choices.why: Each slept its two seconds.

choices.text: The operating system limited the process to 27 threads
choices.why: 27 was the count, not a limit.

choices.text: Waking and ending each one costs real work
choices.why: Right: a million threads are cheap, not free.

prompt: Ten thousand tasks of 100 ms waiting took 10 s on a pool of 100 and 187 ms on virtual threads. What made the difference?
hint: How many could wait at once?

choices.text: Virtual threads sleep less than asked
choices.why: Each slept its 100 ms.

choices.text: The JIT compiled `handleRequest` better the second time
choices.why: The time is waiting, which compiling does not shorten.

choices.text: All ten thousand could wait at the same time
choices.why: Right, instead of a hundred at a time.

choices.text: The virtual run used more processors
choices.why: Same four processors.

prompt: Which programming style do virtual threads make affordable again?

choices.text: Plain blocking code, read top to bottom
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Chains of `thenCompose` for every remote call
choices.why: That is what people wrote to avoid blocking.

choices.text: A thread pool sized by the rule of thumb
choices.why: That is the problem they remove.

choices.text: Parallel streams for I/O
choices.why: Lesson 9 says no to that.

prompt: A database accepts twenty connections. What should ten thousand virtual threads calling it use?

choices.text: A `Semaphore` of twenty
choices.why: Right, or the connection pool's own bound.

choices.text: Nothing: virtual threads queue themselves
choices.why: They would all call at once.

choices.text: `synchronized` around the call
choices.why: That allows one at a time, not twenty.

choices.text: A fixed pool of twenty virtual threads
choices.why: Never pool them; limit the resource instead.

prompt: `Pinning.java` took 25 s on Java 21 and 120 ms on Java 25. What changed in Java 24?

choices.text: Blocking inside `synchronized` stopped pinning the carrier
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The scheduler gained more carriers
choices.why: Still one per processor.

choices.text: `synchronized` was replaced by `ReentrantLock` inside the JDK
choices.why: The keyword is unchanged; the pinning is gone.

choices.text: `Thread.sleep` became faster
choices.why: Each sleep still took 100 ms.

prompt: Which of these gain from running on virtual threads? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A server handling requests that wait for a database
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Resizing images in memory
choices.why: No: that computes too.

choices.text: Counting the primes below two million
choices.why: No: that computes.

choices.text: A crawler fetching ten thousand web pages
choices.why: Yes.
